title: On-demand parameter streaming and fallback heuristics for runtime
summary: Design notes for streaming model parameters on-demand with mmap compatibility and a multi-tier fallback system that trades off latency vs cost. Covers chunking format, runtime residency prediction, safetensors validation, and hot-swap semantics for rollback and experiments.
content:
Context:
This doc captures an experimental approach for serving very large transformer checkpoints with minimal cold-start latency and predictable SLO behaviour. The core idea: avoid loading whole model weights up-front. Instead, stream parameter chunks on-demand to the GPU memory while providing robust, measurable fallback behaviors when IO or memory constraints cause stalls. This is targeted at hosted and dedicated deployments where disk/network can be the bottleneck for large sharded models.

Goals:
- Reduce p99 cold-start token latency for occasional invocations against large, rarely-used models.
- Keep resident GPU RAM usage bounded and predictable via demand-driven residency.
- Provide graceful degradation (accuracy/latency trade-offs) when streaming cannot keep up.
- Ensure safety/integrity: validation of safetensors/blobs, checksumming, and reproducible hot-swap semantics.

Non-goals:
- Replacing full in-memory deployments for high-throughput steady-state workloads.
- Serving extremely low-memory devices (edge); focus is GPU inference tier.

Key concepts and definitions:
- Parameter chunk: an individually addressable contiguous slice of a layer tensor (e.g., a 128MB chunk of attention qkv weights). Chunks are the minimal unit of streaming/mmap eviction.
- Residency map: runtime bitset per model variant indicating which chunks are resident in GPU memory.
- On-demand fetch (ODF): asynchronous request to the IO layer to load a chunk into a staging host buffer or directly into GPU if supported.
- Prefetch hint: speculative fetch triggered by scheduler heuristics based on recent sequence lengths, KV-cache hits, or beam search patterns.
- Fallback variant: a compatible model variant (smaller quantized copy or a narrower architecture) used when streaming-induced stalls would violate latency SLO.

Architecture overview:
1) Model packaging
- Checkpoints are stored as safetensors blobs with an accompanying manifest JSON. The manifest enumerates tensors, chunk boundaries, byte offsets, checksums (SHA256), quantization meta, and compatibility tags (e.g., quantized-int8-compatible).
- Each tensor is logically sharded into fixed-size chunks (configurable, default 32MB). Chunk size per tensor type may vary: embeddings layers prefer larger chunks; attention/kernel tensors use smaller chunks to reduce unnecessary fetches.

2) Startup and mmap compatibility
- When model is mounted, runtime maps the safetensors file read-only via mmap (if the host kernel and FS support it). Mmap provides cheap random access to on-disk bytes and enables zero-copy host->GPU DMA when paired with supported drivers.
- On systems without mmap or where files are on remote object stores, an IO shim presents the same chunk API backed by a local cache that mirrors the chunk layout.
- Validation: on first open, manifest checksums are validated (fast path: validate only header + top-level checksums; slow path: optional per-chunk checks). Validation failures trigger immediate transition to a quarantined state; a quarantine runbook is included below.

3) Residency controller and eviction policy
- The residency controller maintains an LRU+frequency-weighted priority queue of chunks. Priority score = alpha * recent_access_count + beta * recency_weight + gamma * predicted_future_score.
- Predicted_future_score is computed by a lightweight predictor using recent decoding traces (attention heads touched, KV-cache usage, sequence-length histogram) and model topology (which layer tensors are read earlier during generation).
- Eviction is asynchronous: when free GPU memory falls below threshold T_free_low, the controller issues async evict requests to free host staging buffers and optionally writeback (writeback only needed for ephemeral overlay patches; base safetensors are read-only so no writeback for them).

4) Fetch pipeline and latency control
- Fetch flow: scheduler detects missing chunk during kernel dispatch -> enqueue fetch -> probe local host cache -> if miss, schedule remote fetch -> upon arrival, validate chunk checksum -> pin and make visible to GPU execution.
- To avoid blocking critical-path execution, we support three fetch policies:
  a) blocking: stall execution until chunk arrives (used for small missing chunks where stall is acceptable).
  b) optimistic poll: allow execution to continue with a micro-timeout; if not available, issue mid-sequence fallback.
  c) speculative decode: use a conservative approximate patch (see approximations below) to continue and patch later.
- The policy is selected per-chunk by the residency controller based on chunk priority, estimated fetch latency, and the SLO budget remaining for the request.

5) Conservative approximations to avoid stalls
- Zero-fill: temporarily treat missing chunk as zeros for linear layers where this has limited immediate harm (e.g., some adapter layers). Degrades quality but maintains throughput.
- Quantized shadow: keep a lower-precision (int8/4) streamed copy of critical chunks that are fast to load; used as fallback when high-precision chunk is delayed.
- Parameter interpolation: for continuous tensors (e.g., positional embeddings), use interpolation from nearby resident chunks. Use only when validated by eval harness.

6) Hot-swap and experiment overlays
- Overlays: small writeable overlay files live alongside read-only safetensors. Overlays contain delta patches for tensor chunks (e.g., a fine-tune for safety or a small adapter). Overlays are always loaded atomically per chunk and have versioned manifests.
- Hot-swap protocol: to swap to a new checkpoint/variant, the controller prepares new resident map, schedules bulk async fetch for high-priority chunks, then flips an atomic pointer (model instance) used by the scheduler. Any in-flight requests continue against the old instance until completion; new requests use the new instance.
- Rollback: keep last-good manifest and limited number of snapshots. Rollback is the inverse: mark new instance draining, ensure overlays flushed/quarantined, flip pointer back. If rollback fails due to missing chunks, system falls back to a compatible variant.

7) KV cache interactions
- KV cache residency is independent but coordinated: storing KV cache for beam search/long contexts can consume significant GPU memory and interacts with parameter residency.
- Policy: reserve a soft quota for KV cache usage per request class. When KV growth threatens parameter residency for high-priority chunks, trigger conservative eviction of low-priority chunks first (prefer non-attention weight chunks).
- Prefetch hints: when a request begins with a large context, the predictor signals which layer chunks will be needed early (e.g., embeddings + first n transformer blocks). The residency controller prefetches those chunks preemptively into a hot pool.

8) Telemetry and SLO-driven control loops
- Telemetry: per-request metrics include chunk-miss count, average fetch latency, stall time, fallback usage (zero-fill, quant-shadow), and resulting token-level quality deltas (where available).
- Control loops: if the rolling p99 stall time exceeds budget, promotion happens: expand hot pool size, reduce eviction aggressiveness, or swap to a fallback variant. Conversely, if GPU residency is underutilized and cost objective requires reduction, increase eviction aggressiveness, ramp up chunk size, or disable quant-shadow.

9) Safetensors and integrity runbook
- Mandatory: manifest top-level checksum validated on model mount. Optional: per-chunk checksum validation as chunks arrive (configurable for speed vs safety).
- Quarantine mode: if manifest or chunk checksum mismatch, mark model instance quarantined and create an incident ticket with diagnostics (file id, checksum, host path). A quarantined instance refuses to be served; operator can promote a previously validated snapshot.

10) Failure modes and graceful fallback ladder
- Transient IO latency spike: increase optimistic poll thresholds, enable quant-shadow, start speculative prefetch for subsequent requests.
- Sustained throughput shortfall (remote bucket saturated): begin gradual traffic shift to fallback variant with measurable quality delta. Route a sample of traffic for A/B quality checks before full shift.
- Corrupt chunk detected: mark affected chunks quarantined and if a majority of critical chunks are invalid, failover to snapshot or fallback variant.
- Hot-swap conflict (overlay version mismatch): hold swap, notify owner, and optionally attempt automatic three-way merge for adapter patches (best-effort) — if merge fails, fail safe to previous instance.

11) Operational considerations and knobs
- Chunk size tuning: default 32MB; increase for stable high-throughput models to reduce metadata overhead; decrease for models with many small tensors to avoid overfetching.
- Alpha/Beta/Gamma weights for residency scoring are dynamic and tuned via the console (suggested defaults provided).
- Fallback variants catalog: store small quantized variants with validated quality deltas and per-workload rollback recipes in the catalog.

12) Eval and safety tests
- Synthetic microbenchmarks: cold-start generation tests with varying context lengths to measure chunk-miss distributions and p50/p95/p99 fill times.
- Quality regressions: automated eval suites compare outputs from full-resident baseline vs streaming-enabled baseline across prompt suites.
- Chaos tests: inject artificial delays and corrupt chunk payloads to exercise quarantine and fallback ladder.

Open questions / Next steps:
- Predictor design: explore lightweight learned predictors (small LSTM or transformer) vs rule-based heuristics for predicted_future_score. Measure compute overhead and cold-start training cost.
- Direct GPU DMA: evaluate platform support for direct file->GPU DMA from mmap region to further reduce host staging overhead.
- Autoscaler integration: define signals that should influence cluster autoscaling (e.g., sustained high fetch miss rate should trigger additional disk/network bandwidth or reserved capacity).
- Security: evaluate overlay signing and HSM-based manifest verification for enterprise private deployments.

Appendix: quick command runbook (for on-call)
- Detect quarantine: models.list | grep quarantined -> open INF ticket, collect model manifest and host path.
- Force promote snapshot: runtimectl promote --model-id X --snapshot Y (ensures chunk manifests are pre-validated).
- Emergency drain to fallback: runtimectl set-traffic --model X --variant fallback-quantized-1 --weight 100 --grace 30s

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic: mixes heuristic and validated fallbacks. Looking for feedback on chunk sizing defaults, whether overlays should be limited to adapters only, and whether optimistic poll thresholds should be per-layer instead of global.
- Also want validation priority for safetensors: prefer fast mount-time manifest checks in production, per-chunk checks only in high-security tiers.
